identification.summary: Vanilla Tempest is Microsoft's name for a financially motivated ransomware and extortion actor that Microsoft previously tracked as DEV-0832 and that overlaps with Vice Society [S1][S2]. Microsoft's 2022 reporting says activity began as early as June 2021 [S1], while a later Microsoft post says Vanilla Tempest has been active since July 2022 and commonly targets education, healthcare, IT and manufacturing using payloads such as BlackCat, Quantum Locker, Zeppelin and Rhysida [S3]. The actor does not rely on one ransomware family: CISA/FBI/MS-ISAC reported that Vice Society had no ransomware of its own and deployed Hello Kitty, Five Hands and Zeppelin variants [S4]. In 2025 Microsoft reported it was deploying Rhysida after Oyster backdoor infections delivered through fake Microsoft Teams installers [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: June 2021 per Microsoft's 2022 DEV-0832 report [S1]; Microsoft's 2024 post gives July 2022 for Vanilla Tempest [S3]. The two dates are not reconciled in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Vanilla Tempest (formerly DEV-0832); Microsoft's April 2023 update to its 2022 post states the rename [S1]. Aliases Vice Society and VICE SPIDER (CrowdStrike) come from the Microsoft naming map [S8]. Microsoft says separate operators under the DEV-0832 umbrella might maintain their own ransomware payloads, offered as a possible explanation only [S1]. Rhysida is a ransomware brand: Check Point linked Vice Society to Rhysida (shared PortStarter tooling and leak-site timing; a confidence level was not confirmed in this check), and said this does not mean only Vice Society uses it [S7]. Do not merge Rhysida-group facts with Vanilla Tempest facts. Storm-0494 (Gootloader access provider) is a separate Microsoft cluster [S3]. Fox Tempest is a separate Microsoft-tracked malware-signing service [S9].

attribution.confidence: Microsoft assesses the actor as financially motivated and as a cybercriminal group with active ties in the cybercriminal economy [S1][S3]. No source gathered attributes the actor to a state.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident response [S1][S3][S5]; Microsoft's reasoning for the cybercriminal assessment is the shift from a RaaS offering to purchased and custom ransomware [S1]. CISA/FBI/MS-ISAC advisory AA22-249A (September 2022) describes Vice Society as an extortion group first appearing in summer 2021 (via secondary coverage of the advisory) [S4].

objectives: Financial gain through data theft, extortion and ransomware, preferring organizations with weaker security controls and a higher likelihood of compromise and payment [S1]. Some intrusions involved data theft with no ransomware deployed [S1].

sectors: Local government and retail (earlier opportunistic attacks)
targeting.notes: Microsoft says the 2022 activity mainly hit the US education sector, with earlier opportunistic attacks on local government and retail [S1]. CISA/FBI/MS-ISAC said Vice Society disproportionately targeted education, especially K-12 (via secondary coverage) [S4]. Microsoft stated in 2024 that Vanilla Tempest used INC ransomware against US healthcare for the first time [S2]. Check Point found 35 percent of Vice Society victims and 32 percent of Rhysida victims in education (via press coverage) [S7]. Regional scope outside the US is not established in these sources.

capabilities.summary: 2022 (Microsoft): reported initial access through vulnerable web-facing applications and valid accounts, which Microsoft did not confirm; privilege escalation with CVE-2022-24521 and PrintNightmare; LSASS dumping, NTDS.dit theft and Kerberoasting; look-alike admin accounts; lateral movement via RDP, SMB, PsExec, WMI and Impacket; attempts to disable Defender; Rclone and MegaSync for exfiltration; custom PowerShell scripts; SystemBC and PortStarter backdoors; deletion of backups and shadow copies; and password resets for more than 150,000 users [S1]. Ransomware used: BlackCat, QuantumLocker, Zeppelin and variants, RedAlert and a Linux encryptor for ESXi, with a .onion leak site for extortion [S1]. September 2024: access via Gootloader infections handed off by Storm-0494, Supper backdoor, AnyDesk and MEGA, lateral movement by RDP and WMI Provider Host, then INC ransomware [S2][S3]. 2025: SEO-poisoned look-alike Teams download sites delivering a loader and the Oyster backdoor, with payloads signed using Trusted Signing, SSL.com, DigiCert and GlobalSign certificates, ending in Rhysida ransomware [S5][S6]. Microsoft later reported Vanilla Tempest uploaded malicious payloads, including trojanized Teams installers, to the Fox Tempest signing service (via search-result summary of Microsoft's blog) [S9].

campaigns.name: Earliest reported DEV-0832 / Vice Society activity
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says activity began as early as June 2021. CISA/FBI/MS-ISAC describe Vice Society as first appearing in summer 2021.

campaigns.name: Opportunistic ransomware campaigns against US education
campaigns.summary: Between July and October 2022 Microsoft observed DEV-0832 hitting mainly US education, using Zeppelin variants, BlackCat, QuantumLocker and later RedAlert, and in one case resetting passwords for over 150,000 users.

campaigns.name: CISA/FBI/MS-ISAC advisory AA22-249A
campaigns.summary: Joint #StopRansomware advisory warns Vice Society is disproportionately targeting education ahead of the 2022-23 school year (reported via secondary coverage of the advisory).

campaigns.name: Vice Society leak-site activity ends; Rhysida emerges
campaigns.summary: Check Point reports Vice Society leak-site activity stopped after 21 June 2023, correlating with Rhysida's emergence, and linked Vice Society to Rhysida via shared tooling including PortStarter and leak-site timing (confidence level not confirmed in this check; Sophos dates the leak-site stop to July 2023).

campaigns.name: INC ransomware against US healthcare
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed Vanilla Tempest using INC ransomware for the first time against US healthcare, following Gootloader access handed off by Storm-0494, with Supper backdoor, AnyDesk and MEGA.

campaigns.name: Fake Teams installer campaign and certificate revocation
campaigns.summary: Microsoft identified the campaign in late September 2025 and in early October revoked more than 200 fraudulently signed certificates. Fake MSTeamsSetup.exe files on look-alike domains delivered Oyster and ultimately Rhysida.

campaigns.name: Microsoft action against Fox Tempest signing service
campaigns.summary: Microsoft's report on the Fox Tempest malware-signing service names Vanilla Tempest as a customer whose trojanized Teams installers were signed (known here only from a search-result summary of the blog).

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated cybercriminal ransomware and extortion operators; Microsoft notes possible multiple operators under the DEV-0832 umbrella [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: Rotating purchased or affiliate ransomware (Zeppelin variants, BlackCat, QuantumLocker, INC, Rhysida), PowerShell tooling, SystemBC, PortStarter, Supper, Oyster, Impacket, Rclone and legitimate remote-access tools [S1][S2][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: A .onion leak site; hardcoded attacker IPs in exfiltration scripts; payloads staged on hidden shares and domain controllers [S1]; look-alike Teams download domains such as teams-download.buzz, teams-install.run and teams-download.top (named in press coverage) and abused code-signing services [S6].
diamond.victim: Education (mainly US), healthcare, IT, manufacturing, local government and retail [S1][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit-driven extortion that exploits sectors with constrained security resources and high disruption cost [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows Active Directory environments, web-facing applications, VMware ESXi, remote-access services (RDP), and trust in code-signed software and search results for popular collaboration software [S1][S5].

gaps: Microsoft's own 2025 Teams/Oyster/Rhysida blog post was not opened; the 2025 campaign is sourced to a Microsoft Threat Intelligence X post and press coverage [S5][S6].
CISA advisory AA22-249A, Check Point's Rhysida report and the Microsoft Fox Tempest blog could not be fetched; they are cited via secondary coverage or search-result summaries [S4][S7][S9].
The record lists country RU, but no source gathered states a country of origin or any state link. Origin is unattributed here.
Start date conflict: June 2021 [S1] versus July 2022 [S3].
Whether Vanilla Tempest is one team or several operators sharing a name is unresolved [S1].
Confirmed initial access vectors for the 2022 campaign were never verified by Microsoft [S1].

Relationship between Vanilla Tempest and the Rhysida operators is an assessed link only (Check Point; confidence level unverified) [S7]; the Supper backdoor appears in Microsoft's 2024 posts but was not described in detail in sources gathered [S2].
Ransom demands, payments and victim counts for the 2024 and 2025 campaigns are not public in the sources gathered.
MITRE ATT&CK group ID is not recorded for this actor in the encyclopedia.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is Active Directory, domain controllers, backup systems, ESXi hosts and internet-facing applications; remote-access and collaboration software downloads are an entry route [S1][S5]. STEP 2: The actor is financially motivated and favors organizations with weak controls; DoD-adjacent education, healthcare, IT and manufacturing partners (e.g., universities, military health contractors, defense industrial base suppliers) fit that profile [S1][S3]. STEP 3: Observed template is access (web-facing app, valid accounts, Gootloader handoff, or trojanized installer), credential theft, RDP/WMI/PsExec lateral movement, Rclone/MEGA exfiltration, backup destruction, then ransomware and leak-site extortion [S1][S2][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic extortion of weakly defended US education, healthcare and manufacturing organizations with rotating ransomware brands. MDCOA is the same tradecraft aimed at a defense contractor or base-supporting health or education provider, causing mission-system outage and leak of personnel data. Candidate indicators: look-alike Teams download domains and recently signed installers, Oyster or SystemBC beacons, PowerShell scripts on hidden shares with $ names, new look-alike admin accounts, LSASS dumps via comsvcs.dll, mass shadow-copy deletion, and Rclone or MEGA traffic [S1][S5][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track ransomware-brand changes (Zeppelin, BlackCat, INC, Rhysida) as one actor cluster in reporting so rebrands are not read as new threats [S1][S3][S7]. (2) Authorities: response on contractor, university or healthcare networks sits with the owning organization and law enforcement; coordinate through established DIB and DC3 channels rather than assuming DoD authorities [S4]. (3) Mission assurance: protect backups, domain controllers and identity systems, and plan for loss of large numbers of accounts, as Microsoft observed password resets for over 150,000 users [S1]. (4) Coordination: push software-download hygiene guidance (official sources only for collaboration tools) and share signed-malware indicators with the vendor community, since Microsoft revoked more than 200 certificates in this case [S5][S6].

provenance.importedSummary: Vice Society is a ransomware group that has been active since at least June 2021. They primarily target the education and healthcare sectors, but have also been observed targeting the manufacturing industry. The group has used multiple ransomware families and has been known to utilize PowerShell scripts for their attacks. There are similarities between Vice Society and the Rhysida ransomware group, suggesting a potential connection or rebranding.
